reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / WHO Classification of Endocrine Tumours
clinicalPearls: Arises from calcitonin-secreting parafollicular C cells rather than follicular epithelium, so it does not concentrate iodine and radioactive iodine therapy is ineffective
Serum calcitonin is the key tumour marker for diagnosis and follow-up, with carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) as a complementary marker; both track tumour burden
Occurs sporadically or as part of hereditary MEN2 syndromes, so a germline RET mutation should be sought in every patient and appropriate family screening offered
Cytology shows dispersed spindle or plasmacytoid cells with amyloid stroma derived from calcitonin, and immunostaining is positive for calcitonin
Diarrhoea or flushing may occur with advanced disease owing to high circulating calcitonin and related peptides
Total thyroidectomy with central and often lateral nodal clearance is the mainstay, as the tumour spreads early to cervical nodes and the disease is not radioiodine-avid
RET and multikinase inhibitors are used in progressive or metastatic disease, and selective RET inhibitors are effective where a RET alteration is present
reference.pathophysiology: Medullary thyroid carcinoma is a neuroendocrine tumour of the parafollicular C cells, which normally secrete calcitonin. Because it does not originate from follicular epithelium, it neither takes up iodine nor produces thyroglobulin, so calcitonin and CEA serve as its markers and radioactive iodine has no role. Sporadic tumours and the hereditary MEN2 syndromes are both driven by activating RET proto-oncogene mutations; germline RET mutations cause the familial forms and, in MEN2, associate with phaeochromocytoma and, in MEN2A, primary hyperparathyroidism. The tumour deposits amyloid derived from calcitonin and metastasises early to regional cervical lymph nodes.
additionalDifferentials: Parathyroid tumour presenting as a neck mass
Metastasis or neuroendocrine tumour involving the thyroid
additionalInvestigations: Serum calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen as diagnostic and monitoring markers
Germline RET mutation testing with genetic counselling and family screening
Biochemical exclusion of phaeochromocytoma (plasma or urinary metanephrines) before any surgery
Serum calcium and PTH to screen for associated primary hyperparathyroidism in MEN2A
Neck ultrasound with fine-needle aspiration and calcitonin immunostaining
Cross-sectional imaging and functional imaging to stage nodal and distant disease when calcitonin is markedly elevated
redFlags: Coexisting phaeochromocytoma, which must be identified and treated before thyroid surgery to avoid intraoperative crisis
Very high calcitonin with secretory diarrhoea or flushing indicating extensive metastatic disease
Rapidly rising calcitonin or CEA doubling times signalling aggressive progression
Airway or recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement from bulky local disease
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends heavily on stage: node-negative disease confined to the thyroid can be cured surgically, whereas extensive nodal or distant metastasis and short calcitonin/CEA doubling times predict poorer survival.
pitfalls: Proceeding to thyroid surgery without first excluding a phaeochromocytoma in a potential MEN2 patient
Forgetting germline RET testing, thereby missing an inherited syndrome and the chance for family screening
Expecting benefit from radioactive iodine, which is ineffective as C cells do not concentrate iodine
Attributing chronic diarrhoea to gastrointestinal causes and overlooking a calcitonin-secreting tumour
references: WHO Classification of Endocrine and Neuroendocrine Tumours
